extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and advocates of free speech, political philosophy, and public discussion
extracted.subtask_description: Articulating and defending principles that justify freedom of opinion and open discussion, and describing harms of legal or social suppression of beliefs. Emphasizes what proper intellectual and civic practice requires when opinions are formed, taught, and contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on punishing persons for their opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment for holding or promulgating irreligious or heterodox opinions cannot be defended without also justifying historical persecutions (e.g., Socrates, early Christians, Marcus Aurelius's actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that any argument justifying legal penalties for irreligious opinions leads to endorsing past judicial persecutions; defenders of punishment must accept consequences as extreme as those historical cases. Examples and discussion: Socrates put to death for impiety, Christ condemned as blasphemer, Marcus Aurelius persecuting Christianity; the point is that legal punishment for opinion is not defensible by non‑arbitrary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on the idea that truth always triumphs over persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that truth inevitably survives persecution is false; persecution often suppresses true opinions for centuries and can permanently retard their development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cites many historical examples (multiple failed early reform movements, suppression of various heretical groups, successful extirpation of Protestantism in some regions) to show that persecution can and has stopped the spread of truths. Therefore, using the supposed survivability of truth as a justification for persecution is fallacious and cruel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to legal disabilities or exclusions based on belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal doctrines that exclude persons from civic participation or justice because of their religious disbelief (e.g., disallowing atheists as witnesses) are unjust, self-contradictory, and harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill denounces rules that refuse a person's testimony because they do not profess belief in a God and future state (illustrated by 1857 cases), arguing such rules assume atheists are liars and are therefore historically ignorant and practically suicidal; they undermine justice and victimize honest people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from social stigma that enforces orthodoxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Social penalties — exclusion, loss of livelihood, stigma — are as effective as, and often more pervasive than, legal penalties in suppressing opinions and must be resisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where courts no longer execute or imprison heretics, social intolerance forces many to conceal beliefs; this 'social law' prevents public discussion and functions equivalently to imprisonment for most people who depend on public favor or employment. Mill warns this chilling effect is widespread and dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinions must be openly, frequently, and fearlessly discussed
rubrics_metrics.description: For an opinion to be a living truth rather than a 'dead dogma', it must be freely and repeatedly canvassed in public discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If true opinions are not discussed they become prejudices held independent of evidence; Mill contrasts mathematical knowledge (where no contrary is reasonably possible) with moral/religious/political matters that require continual contest to remain vital and understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every person holding an important opinion should know its grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals ought to understand and be able to defend the reasons for their convictions, not merely assent because of authority or habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues the cultivation of intellect requires learning the grounds of one's opinions; on subjects where opposing reasons exist, one must know how to answer objections. He likens this to studying proofs in geometry versus learning moral/political beliefs without hearing objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the strongest form of opposing arguments (devil's-advocate standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: To truly possess an opinion, one must be able to state and confront the best possible objections and hear them presented sincerely by those who believe them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes that hearing opponents only as caricatured or as presented by friends is insufficient; students and citizens should encounter earnest defenders of contrary views in their strongest, most persuasive form so that difficulties facing one’s view are genuinely understood and addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and teaching must expose learners to real adversaries' arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that presents opposing views only as weak or already refuted fails intellectual training; learners must hear and engage with genuine opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill rejects the idea that one can be properly educated about disputed human subjects if pupils never see the objections from those who earnestly hold them; the proper pedagogical method is impartial presentation and active engagement with adversarial reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of thought and discussion is essential to cultivate general intellectual and moral faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread liberty to think and debate is necessary not only for producing exceptional thinkers but for raising the average mental stature and moral courage of a people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill points to historical periods (post-Reformation, the Enlightenment, German speculative movement) where breaking the 'yoke of authority' produced societal advances; suppression leads to timid thinkers, conformism, and narrow practical focus rather than broad principled inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment and timid conformity impoverish public life
rubrics_metrics.description: When heterodox thinkers hide their views or narrow their interests to avoid heresy, public discourse loses vital criticism and innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill describes social reticence leading to either mere conformers or time‑servers; those who avoid intellectual risks narrow their subjects and never produce the 'open, fearless characters' necessary for progress. The loss is not only to heretics but to society at large.

rubrics_metrics.name: If genuine opponents do not exist, simulate them rigorously
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no real adversaries exist, intellectual honesty requires imagining and supplying the strongest counterarguments to test and refine one's convictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill asserts that the discipline of facing the best possible objections (even if only imagined) is indispensable to a true understanding of moral and human questions; in the absence of opponents, one must act as devil's advocate to approximate the benefit of genuine contest.
